{"id": "33669f93-5e91-4a1f-b58a-57895ddd296e", "role": "assistant", "block_type": "tool_summary", "content": [{"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "tooluse_IA447WUWVFIGFVA5sXg8RD", "status": "success", "content": [{"text": "{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"status\":\"SUCCESS\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/quotas-token-burndown.html\",\"content\":\"# How tokens are counted in Amazon Bedrock\\n\\nWhen you run model inference, there are quotas on the number of tokens that can be processed depending on which Amazon Bedrock model you use. Review the following terminology related to token quotas:\\n\\n| Term | Definition |\\n| --- | --- |\\n| `InputTokenCount` | The CloudWatch Amazon Bedrock runtime metric that represents the number of input tokens processed by the model, excluding cached tokens. To determine your total input token consumption against your quota, sum `InputTokenCount + CacheWriteInputTokenCount`. |\\n| `OutputTokenCount` | The CloudWatch Amazon Bedrock runtime metric that represents the number of tokens generated by the model in response to a request. |\\n| `CacheReadInputTokenCount` | The CloudWatch Amazon Bedrock runtime metric that represents the number of input tokens that were successfully retrieved from a cache instead of being reprocessed by the model. This value is 0 if you don't use prompt caching. |\\n| `CacheWriteInputTokenCount` | The CloudWatch Amazon Bedrock runtime metric that represents the number of input tokens that were successfully written into the cache. This value is 0 if you don't use prompt caching. |\\n| Tokens per minute (TPM) | A quota set by AWS at the model level on the number of tokens (including both input and output) that you can use in one minute. |\\n| Tokens per day (TPD) | Maximum tokens per day across all supported Amazon Bedrock models for this account. Token count is estimated based on on-demand pricing; actual token consumption varies by model, input/output ratio, and cache usage. |\\n| `max_tokens` | A parameter you provide in your request to set a maximum amount of output tokens the model can generate. |\\n| Burndown rate | The rate at which input and output tokens are converted into token quota usage for the throttling system. |\\n\\nThe burndown rate for Anthropic Claude models version 4.8 is **15x for output tokens** (1 output token consumes 15 tokens from your quotas) and the burndown rate for Anthropic Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5, Claude Opus 5, Claude Fable 5.1, and Claude Fable 5.2 is **10x for output tokens**. The burndown rate for Anthropic Claude Mythos 5, Claude Mythos 5.1, and Claude Mythos 5.2 is **2.5x for output tokens** (1 output token consumes 2.5 tokens from your quotas). For Anthropic Claude Fable 5 and all other Anthropic models version 4.7 and below, the burndown is **5x for output tokens** (1 output token consumes 5 tokens from your quotas).\\n\\nThe burndown rate for OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-5.6 Terra, and GPT-5.6 Luna on the `bedrock-runtime` endpoint is **10x for output tokens** (1 output token consumes 10 tokens from your quotas).\\n\\nUnless otherwise specified in the model card, the burndown rate for all other models is **1:1** (1 output token consumes 1 token from your quota).\\n\\nToken burndown rates apply only to models available on the `bedrock-runtime` endpoint. Models available exclusively on the `bedrock-mantle` endpoint have separate quotas for input and output tokens, so burndown does not apply.\\n\\n###### Topics\\n\\n* Understanding token quota management\\n* Understanding the impact of the max_tokens parameter\\n* Optimizing the max_tokens parameter\\n\\n## Understanding token quota management\\n\\nWhen you make a request, tokens are deducted from your TPM and TPD quotas.\\nCalculations occur at the following stages:\\n\\n* **At the start of the request** \u2013 The\\n  following sum is deducted from your quotas. The request is throttled if you\\n  exceed a quota.\\n\\n  ```\\n  Total input tokens + max_tokens\\n  ```\\n* **During processing** \u2013 The quota\\n  consumed by the request is periodically adjusted to account for the actual\\n  number of output tokens generated.\\n* **At the end of the request** \u2013 The\\n  total number of tokens consumed by the request will be calculated as follows and any unused tokens are replenished to your quota:\\n\\n  ```\\n  InputTokenCount + CacheWriteInputTokenCount + (OutputTokenCount x burndown rate)\\n  ```\\n\\n  `CacheReadInputTokenCount` don't contribute to this calculation and are not counted toward your quota. If you don't use prompt caching, both `CacheWriteInputTokenCount` and `CacheReadInputTokenCount` will be 0.\\n\\n**Note:**\\n\\nYou're only billed for your actual token usage.\\n\\nFor example, if you use Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4 and send a request containing 1,000 input tokens and it generates a response equivalent to 100 tokens:\\n\\n* **1,500 tokens** (1,000 + 100 x 5) will be depleted from your TPM and TPD quotas.\\n* You'll only be billed for **1,100 tokens**.\\n\\n## Understanding the impact of the max_tokens parameter\\n\\nThe `max_tokens` value is deducted from your quota at the beginning of each request. If you\u2019re hitting TPM quotas earlier than expected, try reducing `max_tokens` to better approximate the size of your completions.\\n\\nThe following scenarios provide examples of how quota deductions would have worked on completed requests using a model that has a 5x burndown rate for output tokens::\\n\\n### Scenario 1: High max_tokens value\\n\\nAssume the following parameters:\\n\\n* **InputTokenCount:** 3,000\\n* **CacheReadInputTokenCount:** 4,000\\n* **CacheWriteInputTokenCount:** 1,000\\n* **OutputTokenCount:** 1,000\\n* **max_tokens:** 32,000\\n\\nThe following quota deductions take place:\\n\\n* **Initial deduction when request is made:** 36,000 (= 3,000 + 1,000 + 32,000)\\n* **Final adjusted deduction after response is generated:** 9,000 (= 3,000 + 1,000 + 1,000 x 5)\\n\\nIn this scenario, fewer concurrent requests could be made because the `max_tokens` parameter was set too high. This reduces the request concurrency, throughput, and quota use, because the TPM quota capacity would be reached quickly.\\n\\n### Scenario 2: Optimized max_tokens value\\n\\nAssume the following parameters:\\n\\n* **InputTokenCount:** 3,000\\n* **CacheReadInputTokenCount:** 4,000\\n* **CacheWriteInputTokenCount:** 1,000\\n* **OutputTokenCount:** 1,000\\n* **max_tokens:** 1,250\\n\\nThe following quota deductions take place:\\n\\n* **Initial deduction when request is made:** 5,250 (= 3,000 + 1,000 + 1,250)\\n* **Final adjusted deduction after response is generated:** 9,000 (= 3,000 + 1,000 + 1,000 x 5)\\n\\nIn this scenario, the `max_tokens` parameter was optimized, because the initial deduction is only slightly higher than the final adjusted deduction. This helped increase the request concurrency, throughput, and quota use.\\n\\n## Optimizing the max_tokens parameter\\n\\nBy optimizing the `max_tokens` parameter, you can efficiently use your allocated quota capacity. To help inform your decision about this parameter, you can use Amazon CloudWatch, which automatically collects metrics from AWS services, including token usage data in Amazon Bedrock.\\n\\nTokens are recorded in the `InputTokenCount` and `OutputTokenCount` runtime metrics (for more metrics, see Amazon Bedrock runtime metrics.\\n\\nTo use CloudWatch monitoring to inform your decision of the `max_tokens` parameter, do the following in the AWS Management Console:\\n\\n1. Sign in to the Amazon CloudWatch console at <https://console.aws.amazon.com/cloudwatch>.\\n2. From the left navigation pane, select **Dashboards**.\\n3. Select the **Automatic dashboards** tab.\\n4. Select **Bedrock**.\\n5. In the **Token Counts by Model** dashboard, select the expand icon.\\n6. Select a time duration and range parameters for the metrics to account for\\n   peak usage.\\n7. From the dropdown menu labeled **Sum**, you can choose\\n   different metrics to observe your token usage. Examine these metrics to\\n   guide your decision on setting your `max_tokens` value.\",\"total_length\":7507,\"start_index\":0,\"end_index\":7507,\"truncated\":false,\"redirected_url\":null,\"error_code\":null}]}}"}]}], "label": "Read Bedrock token burndown documentation page"}

**Why the numbers can't answer this**
- Bedrock publishes these metrics per request. With Statistic Maximum at a 60-second period, each minute gives you the largest single value in that minute. It doesn't give you the minute's total.
- Summing 412 per-minute maximums isn't a token count. It undercuts the real total whenever a minute has more than one request.

**What burndown should look like for Sonnet 5**
The Bedrock docs list **10x burndown for output tokens** for Claude Sonnet 5. Per request, quota consumption is:

`InputTokenCount + CacheWriteInputTokenCount + (OutputTokenCount × 10)`

Cache reads don't count toward the quota.

- Input: 29.08M

- Total: 104.14M, plus any cache-write tokens

That's roughly 3x what you'd see with no burndown (36.6M). Billing stays at actual tokens, so you'd pay for 36.6M and the quota would burn 104.1M.

1. Re-run GetMetricData with Statistic **Sum** for InputTokenCount, OutputTokenCount, CacheWriteInputTokenCount and EstimatedTPMQuotaUsage. Use the same model ID or inference profile dimension and the same period.
2. Compare Sum(EstimatedTPMQuotaUsage) with `Input + CacheWrite + 10 × Output`. They should be close. Differences can come from in-flight `max_tokens` reservations or throttled requests.
3. For peak-minute throttling, compare the per-minute **Sum** against your TPM quota. That's the number the throttler acts on, and it shows whether output burndown is what's pushing you toward the limit.
